12. Clause (6) enables the President to make rules for the allocation and transaction of the business of the Government. In this context, Mr. Afzal admitted that the rules have not been made by the President but he relied upon the Rules of Business which are being followed by the Government for transaction of business in the Secretariat of the Government of Bangladesh. When it was pointed out to Mr. Afzal that the Rules of Business relied upon by him, are not the rules as required to be framed under clauses (5) and (6) of Article 55 of the Constitution but the Rules of Business framed under Article 81 of the Constitution of erstwhile Pakistan which had been abrogated on 25th March, 1969 and limited operation of the same was continued by the Provisional Constitution Order made on the same day, with reference to Article 149 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, Mr. Afzal submitted that the Rules of Business as framed under late Constitution of 1962, being in the category of existing laws, are still in force in Bangladesh. Without expressing any opinion as to whether the said Rules can be treated as existing laws let us examine to what extent presumption of validity can be attached to the order of detention, authenticated by a Section Officer, as provided in Clause (5) of Article 55 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Admittedly the Rules of Business were framed in 1962 under Article 81 of the Constitution of 1962. Article 80 of the said Constitution reads as under:- 

 13. From the Constitution of 1962 it appears that there was no provision of attaching presumption of validity to an order authenticated by an authorised Officer, and there was no pro- vision that validity of an authenticated order could not be questioned in any Court on the ground that it was not duly made. Even if the Rules of Business framed under Article 81 of the Constitution of 1962 be treated as "existing law" being a law in force in Bangladesh, the presumption of an authenticated order and the bar against such order's validity being questioned in a Court on the ground that it was not duly made, cannot be enjoined upon the said Rules of Business on basis of the provision as contained in Clause 5 of Article 55 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. This will amount to adding something to the Rules which was not available to the Rules in the absence of necessary provision in the constitution of 1962. 

 16B. With reference to Section 59 of the Government of India Act, 1935, (Providing to some extent similar provision as contained in Article 55 of the Constitution of Bangladesh it was urged on behalf of the Crown that the orders being on their face regular and in conformity with the language or the rule, it was not open to the Court to investigate their validity any further. It was also urged that the order s had in fact been made in conformity with the provisions of the rule. Section 59(2) of the .Act of 1935 was called in aid in support of the proposition that the validity of the orders must be presumed by the Court and cannot be questioned. Varad Chariar and Zafrulla Khan J. J., took the view that in spite of presumption of the validity the question that was raised on behalf of the detenu t hat the recitals in the order that the Governor had been satisfied that a view to preventing the person from acting in a certain manner, certain act ion was necessary, were not correct can be investigated by the Court. The learned Judges observed that the Court could not be invited to investigate sufficiency of the materials or the reasonableness of the grounds upon which the Governor was satisfied. The learned Judges however, on the authority of the celebrated decisions of the Privy Council, Liversidge Vs. Anderson and another 1942 A.C., 206: (1941) 3 All.
